transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Omar Ruiz (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Ortiz (Sequoia Head of ML), Samir Patel (Infra Lead), Terry Novak (CTO), Priya Menon (Security)

Summary: Technical deep dive on quantization options for Sequoia Robotics. Focus areas: INT8 vs FP8, GPTQ/AWQ toolchains, accuracy regressions, KV cache impact on latency, batching strategies and on-prem/VPC constraints.

--- Transcript Body ---
00:00 Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you all hear me ok?
00:04 Lena: yep loud and clear, thanks Jordan
00:07 Jordan: great, quick agenda, we'll run through the perf numbers, then dig into quantization tradeoffs — INT8/FP8, gptq, awq — and finish with deployment questions for VPC/on-prem.
00:18 Samir: sounds good, we wanna understand how much perf we get vs the accuracy hit, and if kv cache behavior changes when you quantize.
00:25 Maya: absolutely — we'll show some internal runs and talk about kernel selection and batching.
00:30 Terry: quick ask: we have tight latency SLOs on inference path, sub-120ms p95 for short queries; big concern is regression after quant.
00:40 Jordan: noted. ok Maya, you wanna kick off with the numbers?
00:44 Maya: sure, so preliminary: on our 13B baseline, int8 (post-training quant) reduces memory 4x and gives roughly 2.1-2.8x throughput uplift on g4/g5-class hardware; fp8 profiles are a bit more experimental but can get lower dynamic range degradation and often better accuracy than naive int8, but require new kernels.
01:05 Lena: when you say 'int8' are you referring to symmetric per-tensor or per-channel? we saw per-tensor causing big loss on our safety prompts.
01:12 Maya: good call — those numbers are with per-channel quant where supported; per-tensor was worse. also for GPTQ we saw accuracy close to FP16 for many tasks, but there are cornercase regressions on numeric or instruction-following prompts.
01:28 Samir: what's the runtime complexity cost of gptq? i.e., quantize offline and fast at runtime?
01:34 Omar: GPTQ is an offline compression step — you pay time to quantize the model once, sometimes hours per model depending on hardware, but runtime is similar to non-gptq int8 in that kernels can be optimized for the quantized layout. AWQ similarly is an algorithmic q method with better accuracy in many cases but needs specialized kernels.
01:51 Terry: and fp8 is... does it need custom fp8 arithmetic on the GPU? we don't have hardware fp8 support in our datacenter right now.
01:58 Maya: fp8 typically needs either hardware support (NVIDIA Hopper/Ampere variants have some fp8 accel) or emulated fp8 via custom kernels which are slower. so for on-prem without fp8 hardware, fp8 might not be practical.
02:12 Lena: we ran a 200-prompt eval and saw avg rouge/drop ~6% on instruction tasks when using naive int8, but gptq and AWQ narrowed that to 1-2% depending on calibration. is that aligned with your experience?
02:22 Maya: yes that's consistent; AWQ and GPTQ do better on instruction-following. also note that quantization can amplify tokenization edge-cases and safety-related outputs; we recommend targeted calibration and a safety prompt set.
02:36 Priya: from security side, does quantization change data handling or key management? we need to ensure KMS and HSM workflows aren't impacted.
02:42 Omar: quantization is model binary only — it doesn't change key handling. but if you store quantized artifacts in S3 or artifacts storage, you need the same encryption at rest policies. for private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM via our connector; nothing changes functionally for signatures.
02:58 Samir: KV cache — will quantization change KV cache formats or cache hit behavior? we saw larger prefixes giving odd cache misses after a rebuild.
03:06 Maya: good question — the KV cache layout is orthogonal to quantization; cache stores raw activations (or compressed depending on runtime). however, some runtimes choose to keep KV in fp32 to preserve precision even when weights are quantized, which helps reduce accuracy regression for long context. Redwood runtime can choose hybrid: quantized weights + fp16/32 KV cache. that trades memory for accuracy.
03:30 Lena: so if we want to keep p95 latency low for short queries, do you recommend keeping KV in fp16?
03:36 Maya: yes, for short queries the KV size is small; keeping KV in fp16 and quantizing only weights tends to preserve accuracy and keeps latency benefits. for long-context heavy workloads you may want to tune KV caching strategy or use chunked caching.
03:48 Terry: batching — we have bursts, sometimes dozens of short requests. how does batching interact with quantized kernels and latency SLOs?
03:55 Maya: batching increases throughput but adds scheduling latency. Redwood's runtime supports adaptive batching with latency SLOs — we group micro-batches but prioritize sub-120ms SLOs by limiting max batch size and using async dyna-batching. quantized kernels often run faster per-token so you can afford slightly larger batches without SLO breaks, but you must test with your real arrival patterns.
04:18 Samir: curious about kernel selection — do you pick different GEMM kernels for gptq vs awq vs int8?
04:24 Omar: yes, we have a kernel selector that picks the optimal path based on model type, quant format, sequence length distribution and hardware. some kernels are tuned for AWQ layout and others for standard int8. that's why we do per-customer perf profiles.
04:36 Lena: accuracy regressions — you mentioned safety prompt set. can you walk through a regression analysis workflow?
04:42 Maya: we take your representative prompt set and run baseline (fp16) -> quant variants (int8 per-channel, gptq, awq) and compute delta across metrics you care about — e.g., exact match, rouge, hallucination markers, safety flags. we also do targeted adversarial prompts to stress instruction following. we look for both average delta and tail regressions. small avg deltas can hide large tail failures.
05:06 Lena: and what thresholds do you recommend? our product requires 99% pass on the safety test and <2% drop on user-facing accuracy.
05:14 Jordan: from our experience, gptq/AWQ typically meet that with careful calibration; naive int8 often fails the 99% safety pass unless you do per-layer tuning.
05:23 Terry: for POC, what's the fastest way to iterate — do we run Redwood hosted first or go straight to our on-prem?
05:29 Jordan: recommended flow is: 1) run a hosted baseline on Redwood to get quick perf/accuracy numbers (fastest), 2) apply our quantized profiles and run the same evals, 3) once you're satisfied, replicate the winning config into your VPC/on-prem; we provide images and a deployment playbook.
05:46 Priya: for VPC/on-prem we need audit logs, SSO and RBAC. can Redwood console integrate with our SAML provider?
05:52 Omar: yes, Redwood supports SAML/SSO and RBAC for private deployments; logs can be forwarded to your SIEM and we support audit log retention policies.
06:02 Samir: questions about benchmarking: we run on A100/RTX8000 mix; any kernels that require recent CUDA versions?
06:09 Maya: some AWQ/GPTQ optimized kernels require CUDA 12+ and cuBLAS/oneDNN versions; we'll include the exact driver/toolkit matrix in the runbook. For A100 you're good; for RTX8000 we may need specific builds.
06:23 Terry: have you observed quantization causing higher hallucination for knowledge-base lookup style prompts?
06:29 Maya: occasionally, if quantization perturbs logits for rare token patterns. That's why we recommend targeted tuning on domain-specific prompts and sometimes keeping a small number of layers at higher precision (e.g., first and last layers in fp16) — a hybrid approach often reduces hallucination while preserving most perf gains.
06:47 Lena: can Redwood do mixed precision per-layer? we have proprietary prompts that are very brittle.
06:51 Omar: yes, we can configure per-layer precision or layer-groups that remain fp16 while quantizing the rest. It's part of the quant profiles we build per model.
06:58 Samir: how about update/rollout strategy — if we roll new quantized model into production and see regressions, can we fallback quickly?
07:05 Jordan: yes — Redwood supports canary and A/B rollouts with automatic fallback. You can route a small percentage to the new quantized model and observe eval metrics in real time; if safety regressions appear, we can auto-rollback.
07:18 Priya: regulatory: any issues with storing quantized artifacts outside our network? We need to keep certain models on-prem.
07:24 Omar: that's fine — for on-prem/private deployments you keep all artifacts inside your network. For dedicated hosted deployments we can support private model buckets and customer-managed keys.
07:33 Maya: quick note on warm-up and cold-starts: quantized kernels may have slightly different warm-up patterns; ensure your benchmarking includes cold-start passes and also cache warm-up behavior for KV caches.
07:46 Lena: about cache warm-up — we noticed cold-cache p99 spikes; is there a recommended priming approach?
07:51 Maya: yes, we recommend synthetic priming with representative prefixes, or keeping a small warm pool of warmed pods that hold frequently used KV states. Redwood supports warm-pool config for critical routes.
08:03 Terry: ok, walk me through the POC timeline — how long to go from baseline to production-ready?
08:08 Jordan: typical POC: 2 weeks for baseline + eval + runbook, 2-4 weeks to iterate quant profiles and mitigate regressions, then 2-6 weeks for on-prem deployment depending on infra readiness — so roughly 6-12 weeks end-to-end for full production rollout.
08:22 Samir: we prefer a short pilot that proves perf/accuracy first. 2-3 weeks would be ideal.
08:26 Jordan: we can do a fast pilot: Redwood hosted + your eval set in 1-2 weeks to validate; then expand to POC on VPC.
08:33 Lena: any gotchas with tokenization? we saw diffs between fp16 and int8 token probabilities in a few cases.
08:39 Maya: tokenization should be identical; differences come from logits perturbed by quant noise. we log token-level deltas in our regression harness so you can inspect.
08:47 Terry: what's the recommended quant profile for us? 13B instruction-tuned LLM — go GPTQ per-channel + hybrid-KV fp16?
08:54 Maya: that would be our starting recommendation: GPTQ per-channel for weights, keep KV in fp16, preserve first/last layers in fp16 if you see safety regressions, and use AWQ as an alternate if GPTQ doesn't meet accuracy.
09:06 Samir: and cost savings approximate?
09:09 Jordan: depends on GPU class and batch patterns, but ballpark int8/gptq can cut per-token cost by 30-60% primarily via memory reduction enabling larger batch sizes and fewer nodes. We'll put exact estimates in the runbook for your hardware mix.
09:21 Priya: security doc request again — SOC2, encryption, KMS flows, access controls.
09:25 Jordan: we'll attach the security package along with the runbook.
09:28 Lena: for the regression eval, do you require ground-truth labels or accept human-in-the-loop review?
09:33 Maya: either works. for safety we prefer deterministic checks and automated flags, but we'll support a HITL review for edge cases.
09:40 Terry: anything else on on-prem constraints? our infra team wants to know if Redwood images include privileged ops or if we can run in strict unprivileged containers.
09:47 Omar: our on-prem agent can run unprivileged in most setups; some low-level perf optimizations might require device plugin privileges for GPUs. We'll document options and security tradeoffs.
09:58 Jordan: ok let's do a quick recap and owners.
10:01 Jordan: recap - Redwood to send runbook, security docs, and a suggested benchmark config. Sequoia provides prompt set and provisions VPC. Maya/Omar will run initial baseline and quant profiles.
10:12 Lena: confirmed. expect prompts by 7/14.
10:15 Samir: will try to have infra prepped by 7/18.
10:17 Priya: I'll look at the security checklist and get back by 7/12.
10:21 Jordan: perfect. thanks all — we'll follow up with the runbook and links.
10:25 Terry: thanks everyone, good meeting.
